headline: Border Negotiators Agree to Use Game of 'I Spy' to Finalize Himalayan Boundary Claims
body:
Q: The recent border talks were described as 'constructive,' but rumors suggest a pivot from traditional cartography to recreational childhood games. Is this true?

A: It is accurate to say we have moved toward a more kinetic approach. Maps proved to be, shall we say, prone to subjective interpretation. We found that a rigorous, three-day match of 'I Spy' across the ridgeline provides a much more natural sense of land ownership.

Q: How does one determine the actual boundary if the other party spies 'something blue' and insists it refers to a glacier ten kilometers behind your current position?

A: That is precisely why the talks are ongoing. We spent four hours yesterday debating whether the sky counts as a valid object to spy. My counterpart insisted it is a universal constant, while I maintained that for the purpose of a border demarcation, it must be stationary. We are currently drafting a subcommittee report to define the 'stability coefficient' of clouds.

Q: Is there any concern that this might delay the final settlement further?

A: Not at all. We have already cleared the 'Rock' and 'Scree' phases of the game. We are currently deadlocked on a particularly ambiguous patch of lichen, but we’ve agreed to call it a 'trans-border snack' until the next round of discussions in November.
caption: Negotiators have officially swapped satellite imagery for childhood games to settle the border. Expect a final decision once they stop arguing about whether the sky is a permanent fixture. #Diplomacy #BorderTalks #GameNight (satire)
igHook: Who knew global diplomacy was just 'I Spy' with higher stakes?
